#1894. IAN HERBERT: Classless Chuckle Brothers Jason Wilcox and Omar Berrada are not fit to lace Michael Carrick's boots - they have treated a dignified Man United legend shamefully with this painful charade

Published: 07:34 EST, 10 November 2026 | Updated: 03:39 EST, 11 November 2026

Both Michael Carrick and the man who has decided to sack him were present on Saturday night at a 40th anniversary dinner for Sir Alex Ferguson, staged in the dining suite where the Old Trafford dressing rooms used to be. It was lost on no one that Carrick, oozing class and humour that evening, spoke far better than Omar Berrada, Manchester United’s chief executive.

There were 100 or so present and Carrick had just been through the wringer of the 3-2 win over Roma but he did not let his predicament obscure the bigger picture. Carrick ‘spoke brilliantly’, actor James Nesbitt, who was also present, related. ‘The Roma result had just happened, but he showed a real gratitude to Sir Alex. He spoke with confidence and humour, but also with a real understanding of the enormity of what he achieved.’

Those who really understand United would not have been surprised. In the days when it was a classy, brilliantly run club, Carrick was the one who, perhaps more than any other senior player, would always look out for the rank-and-file staff – ensuring that the backroom teams were taken out for a drink at the end of the season, and that taxis home were laid on.

It was he who latched on to what was good about the Manchester United ‘family,’ ensuring that everyone from the reception staff to the laundry team were made to feel a part of it. Sir Jim Ratcliffe’s Ineos have clinically dismantled the old sense of a United ‘community' but Carrick’s return created a gratifying sense around Old Trafford, back in January, that it was perhaps not entirely dead.

All of which contributes to the unalloyed rage that many who love the club will be feeling today about the shameful and classless treatment of Carrick. A man forced through the ritual of driving into the training ground at 7.15am this morning by Berrada and United director of football Jason Wilcox – men not fit to lace his boots – when the whole world knows he is toast.

As Carrick, a professional to his core, went through this painful charade, Berrada and Wilcox – the Statler and Waldorf of the modern Manchester United – had had their secretaries arrange air travel to Monaco today for a meeting with Ratcliffe, which could not be brought forward.

Michael Carrick oozes class and humility but has been dragged through a painful charade by his superiors

Omar Berrada (left) and Jason Wilcox (right) are the the Statler and Waldorf of the modern Manchester United

There have been moments amid the recent tempest which point to United requiring a more commanding manager for the depths that Ratcliffe and his dismal men have reduced the club to. I could see from my vantage point close to the United dugout at their trip to Chelsea, two weeks back, that Carrick simply didn’t have the words to steer the ship away from that afternoon’s disaster.

But in the faces of men like Kobbie Mainoo and, before injury, Marcus Rashford, who have been restored to life and self-belief as United players, we have also witnessed Carrick’s faculty to see and know quality in players and give it full force.

A year ago, we were witnessing Ruben Amorim, the manager hired at vast expense by Ratcliffe’s football geniuses, run down Mainoo’s United career. In the insane mayhem of Sunday afternoon's 4-4 draw against Aston Villa, he was the team’s creative anchor.

The people who have actually mattered at United – the fanbase – appreciate the respect Carrick warrants. It’s why the anthem carrying his name was still coming down from the Stretford End and the old North Stand on Sunday.

And so, of course, does Sir Alex, even though you half suspect he wondered all along if Carrick had quite the bite for the toughest job in world football, while hoping against hope he’d thrive.

‘There is a casualness about him that causes people to misunderstand his value and his constitution,’ Ferguson wrote of Carrick in his autobiography. ‘His handicap was, I feel, that he lacked the bravado of Frank Lampard and Steven Gerrard. But his character has always been outstanding. He's a football man.’ Sir Alex considered Carrick a better player than both those two.

And now what you suspect will be Carrick’s valedictory days at the club he has served so well are presided over by executives whose own fitness for purpose at Old Trafford was an open question from the start.

Very few people around Manchester City viewed the loss of Berrada, their ‘chief football officer’, as something to be fearful about, when Ratcliffe decided to make him United’s chief executive in 2024. Some former City insiders privately wondered how on earth he’d landed a job of that kind.

‘There is a casualness about him that causes people to misunderstand his value and his constitution,’ Sir Alex Ferguson wrote of Carrick in his autobiography

Sir Alex considered Carrick a better player than both Frank Lampard and Steven Gerrard

United want to tell Carrick ‘face to face’ what the whole world knows. These people won’t even discern what gross disrespect they are affording a man who deserves far better

And if Ratcliffe thought he was accessing City’s intellectual property when recruiting Jason Wilcox as technical director, then that was dodgy logic, too. Wilcox had only run City’s academy – a grossly incomparable challenge. His comparable experience to the United role was a mere 15 months as Southampton’s director of football. They were in the Championship for some of that time.

These were the men jetting out to Ratcliffe’s tax haven to tell him who should and should not manage United. Thus subjecting Carrick to another phantom training session at the Carrington – two weeks after watching the Under 21s play there while those Chuckle Brothers put their heads together about sacking him, across the complex.

United are putting it around, would you believe, that they want to be seen to be ‘doing the right thing’ and ‘observing the right process’. Well frankly, many inside football view this leadership group’s decision making as an embarrassment.

Nesbitt expressed sympathy for Carrick. ‘I feel for him,’ he said. ‘I'm no pundit but I am a fan. Clearly there's dissatisfaction with the fans about what we perceive is going on, but I think he's trying his best.’

United want to tell Carrick ‘face to face’ what the whole world knows. These people won’t even discern what gross disrespect they are affording a man who deserves far better.

#1893. Mikel Arteta facing new Arsenal striker selection dilemma after inevitable Viktor Gyokeres goals

Your weekly briefing on Arsenal, featuring team news and expert analysis from Matt Verri

Another Nations League appearance delivered the inevitable for Viktor Gyokeres.

His brace in Sweden’s 3-2 win over Bosnia and Herzegovina made it eight consecutive Nations League games in which he has scored, a record he holds by himself.

Whether Mikel Arteta spent his Saturday night tuned into the action from the Strawberry Arena is unclear, but we know exactly what his thoughts will have been.

Speaking after Gyokeres scored four goals in as many matches in the last international break, Arteta admitted: “Well, the first reaction is, ‘What am I doing that with me they don’t do this, or they haven’t been given the opportunity to do that?’

“That’s a natural one. But then you obviously are really happy.

“I’m very happy that they are able to help the national teams in that way, because I haven’t done it, but it should be one of the best feelings to represent your country and do it in such a way.”

Arteta, then, will be having the same reflections again. How does he get more of the Gyokeres in a Sweden shirt for Arsenal?

Win more penalties would be a good start. Both of Gyokeres’ goals against Bosnia came from the spot and he has now converted his last 29 penalties.

There is also the obvious caveat that the defences Gyokeres is coming up against at international level are not comparable to what he is facing for Arsenal.

As well as his two goals against Bosnia, Gyokeres assisted Alexander Isak’s finish. He ran in behind the high line and squared brilliantly for the Liverpool striker, though the strike was ruled out for offside.

It was perfect decision-making and execution but it was also the kind of space that Arsenal are not afforded on a regular basis.

The Champions League clash with Slavia Prague earlier this month, particularly in the first half, was a rare example of Arsenal being allowed to play with that freedom and Gyokeres delivered probably his best performance in an Arsenal shirt.

However, for all there are obvious tactical differences, the difference in performance levels when Gyokeres is playing for club rather than country is still alarmingly stark.

Gyokeres has had four shots in each of his last three Sweden appearances. Incredibly, he has managed a total of just four shots across 11 matches for Arsenal in the Premier League and Champions League this season.

It has often felt like a confidence issue. Gyokeres looks right at home when leading the line for Sweden. He is the main man, taking free-kicks, penalties, and constantly his team-mates are looking to find him.

The difference in performance levels when Gyokeres is playing for club rather than country is still alarmingly stark

Graham Potter has been important in that, emphasising at every opportunity just how crucial Gyokeres is to the team.

“He’s done brilliant for us when he’s been playing every week [for Arsenal], and he’s done brilliant for us when he hasn’t been playing every week,” Potter told The Independent ahead of this international break.

Gyokeres is not the main character at Arsenal. He knows Arteta will normally turn to Kai Havertz, especially in the big games, regardless of what form the German is in.

Havertz has struggled since picking up a hamstring issue in the last international break but he has still largely kept his place.

Even after Gyokeres played so well against Slavia and continued the big recent improvements in his hold-up play and combinations with those around him, he dropped back to the bench as Havertz started against Hull.

The striker debate is an ongoing one at Arsenal and on recent form, it feels as though the court of public opinion is edging back towards Gyokeres.

That is probably the biggest selection headache Arteta has ahead of Arsenal’s trip to face Newcastle on Saturday.

As the Arsenal boss has admitted himself, he is not getting as much out of Gyokeres as Potter is. For a perfectionist like Arteta, that will be a major source of frustration.

It left now-sacked manager Michael Carrick to field right-backs Diogo Dalot and Noussair Mazraoui in that role in the absence of his two natural options.

Manchester United’s alternative targets to Mauricio Pochettino have been revealed.

Erling Haaland has said he is happy at Manchester City, after commenting on the club’s financial scandal.

During the autumn international break, an independent commission found Man City guilty of all charges related to serious breaches of the Premier League’s financial rules over a nine-season period between 2009/10 and 2018/19.

While City deny any wrongdoing and have launched an appeal, serious sanctions - such as points deductions, fines likely and even expulsion from the Premier League - are likely if that fails.

All four clubs, though, could be trumped by Real Madrid as they retain a buy-back clause.

Bassey is approaching the final six months of his contract at Fulham, so could be available for a cut-price fee.

He told The Athletic: “I’d like to work in England and I met Darren Fletcher and John Murtough.

“It was an interim role and they asked me what I would do once it was over. I told them I would do so well that I would be staying in Manchester, but they gave the job to Ralf [Rangnick].”

#1891. GdS: Club Brugge name price for Tresoldi – why a difficult negotiation beckons for Milan

AC Milan have already discovered the starting price for Nicolo Tresoldi, and it’s safe to say it will not be a cheap deal.

According to this morning’s edition of La Gazzetta dello Sport (seen below), it is no secret that Tresoldi sits at the top of the wish list for Milan. Gerry Cardinale, first and foremost, is a big admirer of the rising Brugge star.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

It is equally well-known that the striker has been a lifelong fan of the Rossoneri. However, his contract runs until 2029, so to take him away from the Jan Breydel Stadium a negotiation is needed with a club that are tough to deal with, as the past shows.

The phone lines between Milan and Brugge were first used in 2022, when the Charles De Ketelaere saga took place. Since then, the management teams at both Milan and the Belgian club have changed, but the history between the two sides should help facilitate discussions. Ardon Jashari was another arduous negotiation, but one that eventually reached the finish line too.

In the cases of De Ketelaere and Jashari, the pitch has arguably favoured the seller more than the buyer. Perhaps the outcome will be different with Tresoldi, should the two parties actually sit down to negotiate.

One caveat: especially in January, the asking is bound to be significant. How significant? Around €60m, according to whispers from Flanders.

Club Brugge are accustomed to selling their best players when the time comes, but they are under no pressure to do so, especially while the season is still underway. Tresoldi has effectively carried the team on his back, scoring eight goals in the league, five in the Champions League, and one in the Super Cup.

The total: 14 goals in 17 official matches. For the club to part ways with their star striker during the mid-season window – a time when all their competitive objectives remain within reach – the offer would certainly need to be more than substantial.

Furthermore, if the 22-year-old forward maintains his current scoring rate throughout the season, his market value will only continue to climb. It is a risk, but also an opportunity. Moreover, Milan are not alone in the race for Tresoldi.

Bayern Munich and top English clubs are keeping a close eye on the former Hannover man, who was born in Cagliari but is a key player for the German U21 national team. Consequently, if Cardinale wishes to beat the competition, he would need to act quickly and decisively.

Tresoldi’s arrival could not see him then become a back-up to Gonçalo Ramos, the most expensive signing in the club’s history. In essence, it requires Ruben Amorim to provide the necessary assurances regarding the wisdom of the acquisition.

Meanwhile, Tresoldi’s hat-trick against Inter at San Siro on October 13th in the Champions League has naturally excited the Rossoneri fans, who would be more than happy to embrace him. However, they aren’t the ones who have to pay the €60m.

#1890. Jesus challenges Portugal to put Denmark defeat behind them

Syndicated reporting provided by Stats Perform and reviewed by the SoccerNews editorial team.

Jorge Jesus insisted his Portugal team remained focused on righting the wrongs from their defeat to Denmark in their final Group A4 clash with Wales in the Nations League.

Portugal have already confirmed their spot in the quarter-finals of the competition and make the trip to the Cardiff City Stadium to face a Wales side guaranteed to finish bottom.

However, the Selecao arrive into Tuesday's encounter off the back of a 4-1 defeat to Denmark, with Rasmus Hojlund and Pierre-Emile Hojbjerg both starring in the victory.

Portugal have not lost back-to-back matches since between September and October 2014 (Albania and France), but have a strong record against Wales in their recent meetings.

They have won four of their five matches against Wales in all competitions (L1), including the last three in a row without conceding a goal, though this is the first time they have been hosted in the nation since May 1951, when they were beaten 2-1.

Jesus' side will finish top of the group if they avoid defeat by Wales, or Denmark do not beat Norway, and Jesus is hoping to see a response from his players.

"When you lose, the focus is on reversing the situation in the next game," Jesus told reporters.

"A 4-1 defeat makes everything heavier, and we can't ignore what we did wrong, but we also can't forget the journey we've been on.

"Nobody talks about the fact that we qualified two matches ago, that we could finish in first place, or that we could end up with 15 points."

— Portugal (@selecaoportugal) November 14, 2026

Portugal have won 12 of their last 16 competitive away matches (D2 L2), and have lost just three of their last 26 on the road in competitive fixtures (W17 D6).

They face a Wales side that have lost four of their last five competitive matches (W1), which is as many defeats as they suffered across their previous 25 (W12 D9 L4) between March 2023 and March 2026.

Wales lost 1-0 to Denmark in their last home Nations League game but have never lost consecutive home games in the competition, while they last did so in competitive games in defeats to Croatia (1-2) and Serbia (0-3) in March and September 2013 respectively.

Despite their progression already being confirmed, Jesus revealed he would not make wholesale changes to his team.

"Throughout this journey, I have always made changes to the team, usually three or four. We have been playing every three days," Jesus said of his potential starting line-up.

"I'm going to replace two or three of the players who have accumulated the most minutes, because I know some haven't fully recovered."

#1889. Arsenal: Jurgen Klopp reveals why he shares Mikel Arteta’s trust in ‘complete’ Kai Havertz

Your weekly briefing on Arsenal, featuring team news and expert analysis from Matt Verri

Jurgen Klopp has hailed Kai Havertz as a “complete” player, as he explained why he shares Mikel Arteta’s trust in the Arsenal striker.

Havertz led the line for Germany in their 3-1 win over Serbia on Saturday, returning straight to his country’s starting lineup after injury.

He started Klopp’s first match in charge of the national team against the Netherlands in September but then missed the next three games during that break due to a hamstring issue.

Despite having limited opportunities to work with Havertz in the early stages of his Germany reign, Klopp has made it clear just how highly he rates the 27-year-old.

“I’ve played against Kai many times, and I can tell you that preparing for a game against him is no walk in the park,” Klopp said.

“You get a real sense of just how complete a player he is. You always have to be prepared for him to produce an outstanding performance because he has all the qualities to do so. He’s a top player.

“Mikel Arteta is someone who, as a person and as a coach, is absolutely determined to win. And unless several negative scenarios all come together, Kai Havertz starts games for Arsenal.

“The fact that he plays here is not simply because I don’t want to leave him out, but because I want to win games.”

Havertz started the season in superb form for Arsenal, scoring in wins over Coventry and Chelsea in the opening weeks of the campaign.

His performances have dipped in recent weeks since the hamstring issue, though Arteta has insisted that injury is not still impacting Havertz.

The criticism of Havertz in the last chunk of matches for Arsenal has been his finishing. Particularly in the Carabao Cup defeat to Fleetwood, Havertz was extremely wasteful.

Klopp alluded to the forward needing more of a clinical touch in front of goal, but he is confident improvements can be made.

“Let’s take the game against Serbia, for example,” Klopp said. “Kai put in an outstanding performance. He could have scored two goals and, under certain circumstances, perhaps even should have.

You always have to be prepared for him to produce an outstanding performance because he has all the qualities to do so

“What interests me is his potential and what we can achieve together with him going forward, rather than dwelling on what has happened so far.

“I’ve watched Kai Havertz – I wouldn’t claim to have seen every single international match, but whenever Kai Havertz has been on my radar, I’ve considered him an absolute top player. So I’m really looking forward to working with him.

“And if there’s anything more we can get out of him, I’m pretty confident that we’ll manage to do that together.”

#1888. USA manager odds: Arsenal legend linked as Pep Guardiola rejects offer to replace Mauricio Pochettino

The USMNT are still on the hunt for a Mauricio Pochettino replacement, with their incumbent head coach days away from taking up the role of head coach at Manchester United.

Plenty of names have been linked to the international job, with Pep Guardiola stunningly reported as the top target. The bookies markets are starting to form, providing odds on recognisable figures such as Thierry Henry, Gareth Southgate, and Julian Nagelsmann.

Argentine boss Pochettino will finish his stint off as head coach of the United States men’s national team with the second leg of the Concacaf Nations League quarter-finals, welcoming Haiti Stateside with a 6-0 aggregate lead in the early hours of Wednesday.

Pochettino will then cross the pond to start life as Manchester United manager, ahead of his first game in charge of the Red Devils against arch-rivals Liverpool on Sunday, November 22.

US Soccer have until March to appoint Pochettino’s replacement, with their next head coach’s first games likely to be the semi-finals of the Nations League.

Former Manchester City boss Guardiola was linked with the role, but after reports he is set to reject any approach from US Soccer, the ex-Barcelona manager has drifted to third with the bookies, at odds of 5/1.

Despite all the star coaches being mentioned with the vacancy, the current frontrunners are two Americans. Nashville SC head coach BJ Callaghan is the favourite at the time of writing, given odds of 3/1.

His fellow countryman Steve Cherundolo, currently in charge of the USA’s Under-23 squad, is second-favourite, priced at 4/1.

Arguably the most recognisable American name in world football at the moment, Jesse Marsch has rather long odds of 30/1. This is explained by his current employment as manager of neighbours Canada, and a history of negative comments towards the USSF.

Pellegrino Matarazzo is another American coach, currently working in Spain as head coach of Real Sociedad in La Liga. Having impressed enough to be given a new two-year deal ahead of this season, Matarazzo is priced at 6/1, reflecting the difficulty of both matching the required compensation and convincing the head coach to leave a job managing in the Europa League.

A host of out of work managers have also been linked to the vacancy. Former England boss Gareth Southgate and ex-Germany head coach Julian Naglesmann have been priced at 25/1, some distance from Thierry Henry and Roberton Martinez - who both sit on odds of 14/1.

Odds according to Canada Sports Betting. Correct at time of publish.

#1887. Manchester United handed huge boost as ‘Mauricio Pochettino begins new job early’

Mauricio Pochettino is set to begin work with Manchester United imminently, with his backroom staff already in the UK.

The Argentine’s assistants, Jesus Perez, Toni Jimenez and Sebastiano Pochettino (Mauricio’s son), all of whom worked with him in the United States setup, flew to England on Saturday to start their new jobs at club level.

The trio will all join the former Chelsea and Tottenham boss in the dugout at Old Trafford with it being reported that the Premier League outfit paid an additional fee to release them from their contracts with US Soccer, following the £7m outlay to secure Pochettino’s services.

The Athletic reports that Perez, Jimenez and Pochettino Jr., immediately travelled to Manchester after the US’ 6-0 win over Haiti in the Concacaf Nations League quarter-finals at the weekend.

That was the first of their two-legged tie, but US Soccer allowed them to depart prematurely as a result of their aggregate lead being so great.

Pochettino will remain in-post for his final match in charge on Tuesday, when the US take on Haiti once more, this time in Cincinnati.

The 54-year-old will leave the US setup just three months after penning a new four-year deal following the World Cup.

Miguel D’Agostino, who has been one of Pochettino’s longest-serving assistants, has remained with his manager for the second leg, but he is also expected to move to Old Trafford when Pochettino begins work officially on November 18, as was confirmed by United.

Pochettino’s first game in charge of the Red Devils will be a trip to Anfield on Sunday, as he looks to guide his new side away from the relegation zone.

#1886. Police 'are trawling through dodgy Fire Stick sellers' bank accounts to contact illegal viewers' of Premier League football and films

Published: 11:08 EST, 10 November 2026 | Updated: 03:40 EST, 11 November 2026

A former detective has revealed the lengths authorities are going to in order to crack down on the use and sale of 'dodgy Fire Sticks'.

Law enforcement organisations across the UK are taking a tougher stance on these devices – and how they are used and distributed – with multiple people having been convicted and jailed in recent years for selling and supplying them.

The devices, which often cost anywhere between £30 and £100 – in comparison with around £30 a month for a Sky Sports subscription – give customers access to a range of premium TV services without paying, most notably in a football sense with access to live matches.

But Rav Wilding, a former detective who recently appeared on the BBC Morning Live show, has sent a fresh warning to individuals that use them.

Wilding said: 'People are buying them online usually on the black market and then they're getting all these services for free essentially.

'But it's a crime. It's not allowed. Owning the stick itself is not a crime, but using it for this purpose is.'

A former detective has revealed the lengths authorities are going to in order to crack down on the use and sale of 'dodgy Fire Sticks'

Wilding went on to say that along with a crackdown on sellers through house raids, authorities are now looking through their accounts to find out in further detail who is using the devices.

They then often contact those users in a new step, with it estimated that around four million people or households have got these Fire Sticks at the moment.

Wilding added: 'All of them are using them illegally. They're going for the distributors. They're going for the sellers. They are having a lot of success. But actually, once they've got the seller, they're going through their accounts.

'They're seeing who has been paying the money for these illegal things, and if they've been paying them for these sticks then people should possibly expect a conversation or two if the police want to know why they've been paying them money for this.'

Wilding revealed that this included checking bank statements to find out the information of individuals who have been paying for such a service, and authorities have been joined by subscription service providers in their clampdown attempts too.

'They (subscription service providers) are losing money to this, so they have been reaching out and are taking action against those people using them illegally as well,' he explained.

'So I wouldn't say it's something you should do. It is actually a crime and it can have a nasty fine, a huge fine and also a custodial sentence for users and sellers of these things.'

Rav Wilding appeared on BBC Morning Live and sent a fresh warning to users of the devices

Daily Mail Sport has previously reported FACT is playing a leading role in the crackdown on the devices, with the anti-piracy organisation liaising with police forces across the country.

And Kieron Sharp, chairman of FACT, added: 'We have a wide range of enforcement options - from issuing cease and desist notices to "knock and talk" visits - through to full criminal prosecutions where appropriate.

'We will take robust action against those involved - not only targeting sellers and distributors, but also those facilitating and profiting from the illegal activity.'

#1885. Ibrahimovic shares feelings on ‘bond’ with Milan: “The most important team in my life”

Zlatan Ibrahimovic has shed light on just how much AC Milan mean to him, labelling it the ‘most important’ club he has represented.

Today marks the launch of ‘Il Milan nel Mondo’, Mauro Suma’s new book exploring the Rossoneri’s reach beyond both Milan and Italy. Several Rossoneri Legends will join the author at the launch this morning, including Daniele Massaro, Demetrio Albertini and Filippo Galli.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

Ibrahimovic wrote a foreword in the book, which has been relayed by MilanNews. The RedBird Capital senior advisor spoke about just how much the club means to him, after his two spells as a player and now his time as an executive.

“Milan are the most important team in my life. And it’s also the only one that convinced me to return. In my career, I’ve worn legendary shirts, played in wonderful cities, and won everywhere. But Milan was something different,” he said.

“It was the only club that truly drew me back, the only one where I felt the need to start over. Convincing Zlatan to return isn’t easy. It’s not easy for anyone. Yet, with Milan, it’s happened more than once.

“This means that between me and these colours, a bond has been created that goes beyond football, beyond trophies, even beyond time. Victory remains in the halls of fame; some teams, however, stay with you. AC Milan belongs to this category.

“The first time, AC Milan brought me happiness, the second, love. In the Rossoneri, I found a sense of belonging that is increasingly rare in modern football. Because starting an adventure with a club can happen. Returning a second time, and then again, means that the club and its fans have become part of you.

“AC Milan are the most successful Italian club at international level, but it’s not just a collection of trophies. It’s an identity. It’s a way of being in football and in the world. Wherever it goes, it leaves a mark. And those who join AC Milan, sometimes, never leave.”

Ibrahimovic signed the first time in August 2010 after an experience at Barcelona that wasn’t a positive one, and he helped Milan to the Scudetto with a 14-goal haul. He won the Capocannoniere the next season, doubling that tally.

He returned in 2019 and scored 25 goals in 37 appearances in his first two campaigns, securing a return to European competitions. At the end of his third season, the climb was complete: the Rossoneri won their 19th league title.

Then, in June 2023 came his emotional farewell at San Siro, before Zlatan returned to the club but wearing a suit and tie.

#1884. Ancelotti swipes back at Romario: ‘He talks a lot’

Syndicated reporting provided by Stats Perform and reviewed by the SoccerNews editorial team.

Carlo Ancelotti took a swipe back at Romario after the latter called for the Brazil coach to step down.

Brazil suffered a 3-2 defeat to Japan on Friday. Vinicius Junior scored twice, but Raphinha was sent off, with Ancelotti also seeing red at full-time.

In the wake of that defeat, Romario – who earned 70 caps for Brazil – called for Ancelotti to quit, posting on social media: "Ancelotti, it's done! Take your things and go."

When asked about Romario's comments ahead of Brazil's friendly against Singapore, Ancelotti said: "In a democratic country with freedom of speech, everyone is allowed to express their opinion.

"He can tell lies, he can tell the truth or talk nonsense.

"It's not up to me to say whether the things he says are correct, wrong or just stupid. The truth is that Romario talks a lot. A lot. It's his right."

#1883. Thomas Frank’s first words as Crystal Palace manager revealed as former Tottenham boss appointed

Thomas Frank has been appointed as Crystal Palace’s new manager after Pierre Sage was sacked last week.

The Frenchman lost his job on Thursday after a disastrous, short-lived spell that dated back as soon as last summer, when he was selected to succeed Oliver Glasner at Selhurst Park.

The Eagles sit bottom of the Premier League table as a result of seven defeats in 10 games, with just two victories.

The south Londoners opted to make a change after their 3-1 home defeat by Liverpool, and they have plumped for the former Brentford and Tottenham head coach as their new boss.

The Dane has signed a two-and-a-half year deal in south London, and he hailed his new side as “iconic” in his first words in his new position.

"It's an honour to sit here and be in charge of this fantastic football club,” Frank told Palace’s club media upon his appointment announcement.

“I'm really, really looking forward to it.

"Crystal Palace is an iconic club in England and in the Premier League. I will do everything I possibly can to help and support the players and everyone around the place, and I'm really looking forward to meeting them.”

Frank’s first game in charge of his new side will come against Coventry City on Saturday, as the Eagles travel to Warwickshire looking for just their third victory of the campaign.

A home Europa League encounter with Real Sociedad will follow as the new head coach takes his bow in front of the Selhurst support, and a first home league game follows next weekend, when newly-promoted Hull City travel to the capital.

#1882. Thomas Frank’s biggest Tottenham mistakes as Crystal Palace announce new manager

Your weekly briefing on Tottenham, featuring team news and expert analysis from Sam Tabuteau

Thomas Frank succeeds Pierre Sage as Crystal Palace manager, signing a two-and-a-half-year deal with the south-east London club.

The Dane will be in the dugout for Palace’s trip to Coventry on Saturday, returning to management for the first time since leaving Tottenham in February.

Frank was on the Eagles’ shortlist to take over from Oliver Glasner this summer before they opted for Sage, and the former Spurs and Brentford boss is said to have been keen on a return to the Premier League.

After a difficult spell in north London, with the club sitting narrowly above the relegation zone when he left, Frank took time away from management to learn from leaders inside and outside football, as well as spending time with friends and family.

His disastrous stint at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium has inevitably left some scars, but Frank is still widely revered for his work in the west of the capital, where he got the Bees promoted to the Premier League, stabilising them as a top-flight club on one of the division’s lowest budgets.

Frank will undoubtedly have learnt some lessons from his seven-month spell at Spurs.

Here, Sam Tabuteau identifies the three biggest mishaps of Frank’s Tottenham tenure…

Part of what made Frank such an engaging character at Brentford was his ability to talk openly and honestly about the club’s culture, tactics and wider societal issues while maintaining an endearingly British sense of humour.

At times self-deprecating and sarcastic, Frank earned plenty of admirers for the way in which he humanised what can often be a cut-throat and emotionally vacant industry.

After nine years at Brentford, nearly seven as head coach, Frank had earned the luxury of being able to talk so candidly. He was comfortable in his surroundings, and safe in the knowledge that Brentford had not sacked a manager since 2015.

However, at Tottenham, he was starting from scratch at a club whose ambitions don’t leave much room for home truths.

Coming off the back of their Europa League triumph, Spurs supporters wanted to hear how the club was going to push forward.

Yet in his first press conference as Spurs manager, Frank joked that if there was one thing he could promise, it was that they would lose games.

Frank appointed new Crystal Palace manager

Frank’s first words as Palace manager as former Spurs boss appointed

Arteta facing new Arsenal dilemma after inevitable Gyokeres goals

Discover a hidden island paradise in the Indian Ocean

His ill-timed quip did not go down well, regardless of the spirit in which it was intended, and from that point on Frank was fighting a losing battle to convince supporters he understood the culture of the club.

Losing supporters after tame Chelsea defeat

Given how it ended, Frank’s tenure started surprisingly positively, with Tottenham third in the Premier League table after nine games.

The mood quickly changed, though, after a dispiriting 1-0 home defeat to London rivals Chelsea, in which Spurs managed just one shot on target.

Frank’s pragmatic style worked well at Brentford because they had one of the most efficient frontlines in the division and were not expected to dominate possession.

At Spurs, however, Frank’s risk-averse style combined with an attacking unit missing Dejan Kulusevski and James Maddison meant they relied heavily on set-piece goals and struggled to create chances in open play.

Frank’s inability to evolve his style, coupled with Spurs’ shortcomings in attack, culminated in a performance against Chelsea that left many supporters disillusioned and would come to symbolise his time in charge.

Another example of Frank’s naivety came during January’s stoppage-time defeat to Bournemouth, when the 53-year-old was pictured pre-match walking around the pitch at the Vitality Stadium with an Arsenal-branded coffee cup.

Seemingly none the wiser, Frank stood with the cup in hand while some staff members could not hide their shock, and the resulting pictures went viral as Spurs slumped to an excruciating defeat.

After the game, Frank’s blunder took centre stage, and his mystified reaction just about summed up the growing rift between him and Spurs’ supporters.

While Spurs fans vented their anger and embarrassment online and in the stands, Frank could not begin to understand how an innocent mistake could be blown so far out of proportion.

From that point on, it was clear that the narrative was quickly beginning to slip from Frank’s grasp and Spurs would lose their next five league games before he was relieved of his duties.

#1881. Epigenetic heterogeneity in breast tumours informs diagnosis and prognosis

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Breast cancer, the most diagnosed cancer among women, is stratified by gene expression patterns into luminal and basal-like subtypes, and the latter is associated with worse prognosis1,2,3. Recent advances in single-cell technologies have underscored the presence of intratumour heterogeneity, which poses substantial challenges in cancer treatment and achieving long-term disease-free survival4,5,6,7. Here we extensively profile epigenetic heterogeneity in a cohort of treatment-naive human luminal tumours, which were obtained directly after surgical resection. By applying a single-cell epigenetic approach based on cytometry by time-of-flight, we identify a recurrent subpopulation of basal-like cells in luminal tumours with a conserved epigenetic signature across patients. These basal-like cells, also identified by deconvolution of whole-genome DNA methylation patterns, are characterized by high expression of aggressive oncogenic traits and downregulation of hormone receptor signalling. Direct comparison of single-cell proteomic and genomic profiling of monomethylation and trimethylation of histone 3 on lysine 4 revealed that these marks are key features associated with loss of luminal identity. Finally, we highlight the potential of concomitant single-molecule profiling of histone modifications on cell-free nucleosomes in blood as an epigenetic liquid biopsy approach for early diagnosis of breast cancer. Moreover, the epigenetic basal signature measured in blood is linked to prognosis, which enables the identification of patients at increased risk for disease relapse.

Gene expression profiles classify breast cancers into luminal A or luminal B (hormone-receptor-positive (HR+)), HER2-positive and basal-like subtypes. Among these, basal-like subtypes largely overlap with triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC)2,3. These classifications guide treatment management and prognosis. Luminal HR+ breast cancer generally responds to endocrine therapy with favourable outcomes, yet many patients relapse8. Single-cell and spatial studies have revealed substantial intratumoural heterogeneity among subtypes, which potentially drive treatment resistance and recurrence4,5,6,7,9.

Chromatin organization, mediated by DNA and histone post-translational modifications (PTMs), facilitates the acquisition of epigenetically distinct cellular states in genetically identical cells10,11,12. Although single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) and single-cell chromatin-accessibility sequencing (scATAC–seq) delineate intratumour heterogeneity13,14,15,16, the contribution of chromatin patterns remains unclear17. Single-cell profiling of histone marks, such as trimethylation of histone 3 on lysine 27 (H3K27me3), implicates chromatin states in breast tumour heterogeneity and treatment resistance18,19. However, these methods measure a limited number of chromatin marks, which hinders analyses of complex patterns and interactions. We developed a cytometry by time-of-flight (CyTOF) method to systematically profile multiple histone PTMs and decode population-specific chromatin patterns to examine heterogeneity among cancer cells20,21,22,23.

Tumour epigenetic states are also reflected in blood. Cell-free, plasma-circulating nucleosomes, released mainly by dying normal and cancer cells, retain tissue-of-origin epigenetic patterns24,25,26,27. Our single-molecule imaging platform, epigenetics of plasma isolated nucleosomes (EPINUC), captures multiple epigenetic features on plasma nucleosomes28. This method detects colorectal cancer, including low-burden early-stage disease28, and enables minimally invasive molecular profiling and treatment monitoring of paediatric brain tumours29.

Here we present a holistic epigenetic analysis of primary treatment-naive breast tumours and blood cell-free nucleosomes. Linking recurrent intratumoural epigenetic patterns to circulating nucleosomes connects tumour epigenetic heterogeneity with its potential clinical implications. This work reveals epigenetic alterations as key mediators of intratumour heterogeneity and potential biomarkers for early diagnosis and prognosis.

To assess heterogeneity in breast tumour histone modifications, we performed epigenetic focused CyTOF on fresh, surgically resected tumours from treatment-naive women and quantified histone modifications at single-cell resolution (Fig. 1a and Supplementary Table 1). The cohort included mainly luminal HR+ tumours and only one basal triple-negative (TN, HR–) tumour (n = 12; Supplementary Table 2 and Supplementary Fig. 1a,b), as standard neoadjuvant therapy excluded most TN cases from treatment-naive eligibility. Following batch correction and normalization, uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) analysis of all 12 tumours revealed that tumour cells largely occupied patient-specific regions, whereas stromal cells clustered together across patients. This result aligns with previous studies that measured single-cell genomic differences13,14 (Fig. 1b, Methods and Supplementary Fig. 2a). Partial overlap among luminal tumour cells from different patients probably reflects shared lineage-specific epigenetic programs. As expected, stromal cells expressed vimentin and αSMA, whereas tumour cells expressed the epithelial keratins, EpCAM and E-cadherin (Fig. 1b,c and Supplementary Fig. 2b,c). Notably, the basal TN tumour differed from HR+ tumours, showing low expression of the luminal marker GATA3 and high expression of the basal marker cytokeratin-5 (K5; also known as KRT5) and mesenchymal vimentin markers (Fig. 1b,c and Supplementary Fig. 2d). Stromal and tumour chromatin patterns also differed, a result that underscores their role in dictating cellular identity (Fig. 1d and Supplementary Fig. 2e). CyTOF analysis of MCF7 (luminal) and four basal-like TN cell lines validated that GATA3 and K5 expression patterns can differentiate luminal and basal-like identities. Moreover, SHAP analysis30,31 identified these two markers as the strongest discriminators of tumour type (Fig. 1e,f). Using multiple cell-identity markers, we derived a PermCell luminal signature (Methods) that accurately distinguished the identities of the cell lines (Fig. 1g).

a, Schematic of the experiment. Tumours were dissociated, depleted of CD45+ immune cells, stained with metal-conjugated antibodies and analysed by CyTOF (Supplementary Table 1). Ac, acetylation; Me, Methylation; Ub, Ubiquitination. b, UMAP of the CyTOF dataset (1,157,765 cells, n = 12 tumours, mean of 96,480 cells per tumour; Supplementary Table 3). Shown are around 1,000 cells per sample (one replicate per tumour), coloured by sample (left) or marker intensity (right). Dashed outlines indicate HR+, TN and stromal cell regions. c,d, Heatmaps of mean marker levels in stroma, TN tumour (n = 1) and luminal tumours (n = 11); rows are standardized and clustered. e, UMAP of breast cancer cell lines. Shown are 5,000 cells per line, coloured by line (left) or marker intensity (right). f, XGBoost classifier segregating luminal and basal-like cell lines using all cell identity markers (Supplementary Table 1). SHAP scores indicate feature importance. g, UMAP as in e, coloured by a luminal signature score derived from the indicated markers (bottom). Asterisk indicates markers absent from the cell-line panel. h, UMAP of cells from tumour 5 (representative of n = 11) following DBSCAN clustering and noise (unclassified cells) removal, coloured by subpopulation, marker intensity and luminal signature. i, Heatmap of mean marker levels per subpopulation in h, row-standardized as z-scores. Rows and columns are clustered. j, UMAP of two luminal PDX models, coloured as in h. For PDX-1, six tumours were sampled equally to match PDX-2 cell numbers. k,l, Mean CyTOF Ki-67 levels versus the percentage of Ki-67+ cells by IHC (k) or cycling cells by epigenetic signature (l, n = 11). Data show linear fit (lines), 95% confidence intervals (CI, grey), Pearson’s r and two-sided P values. Tumour 20 showed outlier CyTOF Ki-67 levels and was excluded. m,n, UMAP and DBSCAN clustering of MCF7 parental cells (m) and a single-cell-derived clone (n, clone 5, using only epigenetic features, coloured as in h.Results were reproduced in seven independent MCF7 CyTOF experiments and three independently derived clones (Extended Data Fig. 2). Schematic in a created in BioRender; Furth, N. https://biorender.com/twf1psb (2026).

We next examined intratumour heterogeneity, focusing on the cancer cells of each luminal breast tumour separately. UMAP clustering and density-based spatial clustering of applications with noise (DBSCAN) across all features revealed three subpopulations in each tumour, which we termed cycling, luminal and basal-like (Fig. 1h,i and Extended Data Fig. 1a,b). These subpopulations were also conserved in two different luminal patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models. This finding validates the observed heterogeneity as an inherent feature of luminal breast tumours and excludes contamination of normal cells (Fig. 1j and Extended Data Fig. 1c). MCF7 cells showed similar luminal and basal-like heterogeneity, although most cells were cycling, as expected for a cell line (Extended Data Fig. 1d). In tumours, only a luminal subset cycled and expressed high levels of Ki-67, a result consistent with previous immunohistochemistry (IHC) and scRNA-seq studies14,32. CyTOF Ki-67 levels correlated with pathology estimates (Fig. 1k). Cycling cells also showed high levels of multiple chromatin modifications, both in raw measurements and following normalization to core histones (Fig. 1i, Extended Data Fig. 1a–c and Supplementary Fig. 3). We validated this result by repeating CyTOF analyses of two tumours (14 and 18), adding the established cell cycle marker phospho-Rb (pRb). pRb-positive cells showed an increase in core histones, as expected from cycling cells, and a larger increase in histone PTMs (Supplementary Fig. 3). Accordingly, the epigenetically inferred cycling fraction strongly correlated with Ki-67 levels (Fig. 1l).

Most cancer cells strongly expressed GATA3 and scored highly for the luminal signature, consistent with clinical classification (Fig. 1h, Extended Data Fig. 1a,b and Supplementary Fig. 4a). Moreover, in each tumour, the PDX samples and the MCF7 cells, we identified a minor recurrent subpopulation that acquired basal-like identity, with high K5 expression and a reduced luminal signature (Fig. 1h–j, Extended Data Fig. 1 and Supplementary Fig. 4a). This phenotypic diversity is consistent with previous single-cell studies of human and mouse breast tumours14,21,33,34. Notably, luminal and basal-like cells also had distinct histone PTM signatures (Fig. 1h–j and Extended Data Fig. 1). Accordingly, UMAP plots based solely on histone modifications revealed separation of the subpopulations, which validated the epigenetic basis of this phenotypic diversity (Supplementary Fig. 4b). In MCF7 cells, epigenetic UMAP and clustering similarly identified several clusters, including a K5hi basal-like population (Fig. 1m). These basal-like cells with reduced luminal signalling appeared closer in UMAP space to the TN cell lines, which provided further support for their basal-like identity (Supplementary Fig. 4c). Independent CyTOF experiments, additional MCF7 parental cell culture and populations derived from independent single-cell clones revealed similar subpopulation patterns, a result that argues against a genetic basis for these effects (Fig. 1n and Extended Data Fig. 2a–c). Moreover, individual PDX tumours derived from the same donor and grown independently in different mice showed similar subpopulation proportions, which provides support for a dynamic and plastic relationship between cell states (Extended Data Fig. 2d). Overall, our data revealed inherent intratumour heterogeneity in luminal tumours, with epigenetic variability between distinct subpopulations.

We further explored the characteristics of the cycling, luminal and basal-like subpopulations. Unsupervised clustering grouped corresponding subpopulations across patients, which confirmed their robustness and similarity (Fig. 2a). Across tumours, luminal cells expressed oestrogen receptor (ER), GATA3 and cytokeratin-8 and cytokeratin-18 (K8/18; also known as KRT8 and KRT18, respectively), whereas basal-like cells downregulated these luminal markers and highly expressed K5 (Fig. 2b). As these subpopulations also exhibited distinct and conserved chromatin patterns, we applied a machine-learning algorithm to predict intratumour classification35. In each tumour, a model trained on a random subset predicted the remaining cells with 94% accuracy, which confirmed the robust differences between subpopulations (Fig. 2c and Extended Data Fig. 3a). It also assigned 78% of unclustered ‘noise’ cells with >95% confidence, generating classifications that aligned with the original clustering and UMAP positions (Extended Data Fig. 3b). SHAP analysis identified the features driving each subpopulation. In detail, histone PTMs, particularly the four acetylation marks, were leading predictors of cycling cells despite overlap of individual marks with basal-like cells (Extended Data Fig. 3c,d). Polycomb-associated H3K27me3 and H2Aub also contributed to the features, a finding consistent with previously observed Polycomb deregulation and pro-proliferative activity in breast cancer36,37,38.

Luminal and basal-like separation was similarly epigenetic driven, with H4K20me3, H3K36me3 and H3K9me2 marks having the highest SHAP scores (Fig. 2d). Across tumours, basal-like cells consistently had increased H3K9me2 and H3K4 monomethylation and trimethylation, whereas luminal cells had enhanced H4K20me3, H3K36me3, H3K9me3 and H3K27me3 marks (Fig. 2e). These results align with subtype-associated histone PTM signatures39 and reported roles for H3K4 demethylases, such as JARID1B, in luminal–basal transitions40. Both luminal and basal-like cells showed similar pRb distribution, which provide support for the conclusion that these results reflect distinct cell states rather than cell cycle differences (Extended Data Fig. 3e). Similar epigenetic signatures distinguished luminal and basal-like populations in PDX models (Extended Data Fig. 3f). Accordingly, epigenetic-only basal-like PermCell scores accurately captured basal-like cells in tumours, PDXs and MCF7 cells (Fig. 2f and Extended Data Fig. 4). Overall, our computational framework confirms that there is recurrent epigenetic heterogeneity in HR+ breast tumours and highlight chromatin patterns associated with basal-like K5hi cells.

Consistent with the CyTOF results, tumours with higher fractions of epigenetically defined basal-like cells had fewer ER-positive and progesterone receptor (PR)-positive cells, as measured by IHC (Extended Data Fig. 5a,b and Supplementary Table 2). Basal-like cells were also more abundant in worse-prognosis luminal B than luminal A tumours. This result is in agreement with studies showing that these tumours exhibit features shared with the basal-like subtype3,41,42,43 (Fig. 2g). Although tumour mutational burden was low across the cohort, it correlated positively with the CyTOF-defined basal-like fraction, which parallels the greater genomic instability typically associated with TNBC44,45 (Fig. 2h and Supplementary Table 2). TP53 mutant tumours likewise contained more basal-like cells (Extended Data Fig. 5c), a finding reminiscent of single-cell studies of glioblastoma showing that genetic mutations may affect balance between cellular states46. Overall, these associations between pathological and molecular characteristics link the epigenetically distinct basal-like subpopulation to a more aggressive disease phenotype.

To characterize these cells functionally, we performed FACS to sort cells from tumour 19 and then low-input mass spectrometry. After excluding stroma through pan-cytokeratin staining, cells were sorted according to K5 levels to enrich for basal-like cells compared with the luminal population. K5low cells highly expressed luminal markers and proteins associated with oestrogen signalling, whereas basal-like K5hi cells expressed proteins involved in oncogenic pathways, such as MYC–mTOR signalling (Fig. 2i–k). Moreover, multiple chromatin regulators differed between these subpopulations, including the H3K4me1 methyltransferase SETD7 and histone demethylase KDM4A, consistent with the histone PTM differences observed by CyTOF47,48 (Extended Data Fig. 5d). KDM4A, enriched in K5hi cells, targets H3K9me3 and H3K36me3, which potentially accounts for their reduced levels and H3K9me2 accumulation in the basal-like population49. Comparisons with a normal mammary single-cell atlas50 revealed hormone-sensing programs in K5low cells and an alveolar progenitor signature in K5hi cells (Fig. 2l), a result consistent with their enrichment in luminal and basal TN tumours, respectively50.

To gain a mechanistic understanding of these findings, we sorted MCF7 cells using K5-specific and GATA3-specific antibodies and performed transcriptomic profiling, comparing basal-like cells (K5hiGATA3low) to bulk MCF7 or extreme luminal cells (K5lowGATA3hi; Extended Data Fig. 5e,f). Notably, basal-like cells were enriched for epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) genes (P < 0.05; Extended Data Fig. 5f). We then focused on differentially expressed cell surface markers to enable live sorting, which revealed that CD74 was significantly upregulated in basal-like cells in both MCF7 and tumour 19 proteomic analyses (Fig. 2m and Extended Data Fig. 5g). Live-sorted CD74hi cells exhibited increased migratory capacity in migration and wound-healing assays, which provided further support for the more aggressive phenotypes of basal-like cells (Fig. 2n,o and Extended Data Fig. 5h). Together, these single-cell and bulk proteomics and functional assays identify epigenetically distinct K5hi basal-like cells in luminal tumours associated with aggressive traits such as reduced luminal signalling, elevated oncogenic signalling and increased migratory potential.

The distinct chromatin and phenotypic states of the basal-like subpopulation led us to explore whether intratumour epigenetic heterogeneity is also apparent in DNA methylation patterns. Thus, we conducted deep whole-genome bisulfite sequencing (WGBS) on three luminal tumours from our cohort. DNA methylation patterns accurately capture breast cancer subtyping, as shown by The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA)51. We next jointly deconvoluted the TCGA and our WGBS data into functional archetypes (V1–V3), with each tumour positioned in the deconvolution space. Stratifying the data into three archetypes revealed the expected separation of basal (TN) tumours from luminal (HR+), with archetype V3 associated with basal tumours (Extended Data Fig. 6a). Tumours 18, 19 and 23 from our cohort clustered with the luminal tumours, as expected from their bulk clinical subtyping. Correlation of the archetype contribution with RNA expression confirmed the association of V1 and V2 with luminal transcriptional programs, whereas V3 was associated with EMT, a result consistent with previous studies of TN tumours52,53,54 (Extended Data Fig. 6b and Supplementary Fig. 5a). To improve resolution, we added a fourth archetype (V4). This analysis revealed another layer of diversity: basal TN tumours were strongly associated with V3, which corresponded with reduced oestrogen signalling and increased oncogenic signalling, whereas luminal tumours were more heterogeneous and spread across the V1 axis (Fig. 3a,b and Supplementary Fig. 5b). Notably, V1 was strongly enriched for EMT, thereby potentially capturing an intermediate-transitional state between luminal and basal-like programs. Moreover, the percentage of CyTOF-measured, vimentin-positive cells, indicative of EMT, in tumours 18 and 19 differed accordingly (Fig. 3c and Supplementary Fig. 5c). Tumour 19, with a higher V1 contribution, also comprised more vimentin-positive cells, as assessed by CyTOF. These results support the use of WGBS deconvolution to capture functionally distinct cellular states in tumours, such as luminal cells undergoing EMT.

To directly link the CyTOF-defined subpopulations with DNA methylation patterns, we sorted K5hi and K5low cells from tumour 5 and tumour 23, followed by enzyme-mediated methylation sequencing (EM-seq). Functional enrichment of differentially methylated promoters revealed hypermethylation of oestrogen-response programs in K5hi cells, whereas genes associated with aggressive and oncogenic features, including KRAS signalling and mesenchymal or basal-state transitions, were hypomethylated (Extended Data Fig. 6c,d). We next derived a CpG island (CGI) methylation signature to distinguish the two states using CGIs that were concordantly differentially methylated across both tumours. In TCGA breast cancer data, this signature scored higher in basal-like tumours, which indicated that the K5hi methylation program resembles basal-like tumours (Extended Data Fig. 6e). K5hi samples also showed higher contribution to the basal-associated and EMT-associated archetypes than K5low samples, in both the three-archetype and four-archetype models (Extended Data Fig. 6f,g). Thus, the CyTOF-defined basal-like population exhibits basal-like and EMT-related methylation programs, which reveals another layer of intratumoural epigenetic heterogeneity.

Having identified distinct DNA methylation programs associated with tumour cell states, we next assessed cell-to-cell variability by clustering read-level methylation patterns across 100-bp genomic bins and calculating empirical entropy as an estimation of cell-type heterogeneity55. Genes near high-entropy bins were associated with functional terms related to poor differentiation, tumour aggressiveness and basal compared with luminal identity (Supplementary Fig. 6a). This result suggests that empirical entropy, by capturing diverse DNA methylation states, can be used as a proxy for cell-to-cell heterogeneity and reveal functional differences between subpopulations. We next calculated the mean entropy for each CGI (Extended Data Fig. 7a). As expected, most CGIs were unmethylated across all cells56, thus showing zero entropy. The variable CGIs (entropy > 0) were functionally enriched for EMT and the related Hedgehog signalling pathways, which indicated that these are differentially regulated in tumours57 (Extended Data Fig. 7b). This analysis suggests that intratumour variability in methylation patterns may be associated with cell identity transitions.

To further explore intratumour entropy and its relation to cell identity, we leveraged a published multiomic study of luminal breast cancer that included single-cell expression and chromatin accessibility measurements13. Focusing on cancer cells, we observed intratumour heterogeneity in luminal and basal-like expression patterns, as previously described14,54 (Supplementary Fig. 6b). Using the ATAC–seq modality, we calculated the within-peak (WIP) fraction, a metric of epigenetic noise58, whereby a low-WIP fraction may indicate a destabilized or noisier epigenome, which supports cell plasticity. For each tumour, we correlated the WIP fraction with chromatin accessibility of basal-like and luminal gene signatures. Cells that scored high for EMT and basal-like identity showed lower WIP fraction, a finding reminiscent of the higher DNA methylation entropy associated with these signatures (Fig. 3d and Supplementary Fig. 6c). Single-cell multiome analysis of a freshly resected independent luminal tumour reproduced the basal–luminal continuum and association between basal identity and reduced WIP fraction (Supplementary Fig. 6d,e). To explore whether the increased epigenetic noise is associated with higher transcriptional heterogeneity, we divided cells into quartiles according to a published basal–luminal index59 and basal-like and luminal gene sets (Methods). Indeed, across all tumours, cells with a high basal identity showed higher transcriptional heterogeneity (Extended Data Fig. 7c). In line with these observations, the CyTOF-defined basal-like subpopulation also showed higher epigenetic heterogeneity (Extended Data Fig. 7d). Moreover, read-level methylation entropy was higher in K5hi-sorted compared with K5low-sorted populations in both tumours analysed by EM-seq, with higher variability among the K5hi 200-cell replicates (Supplementary Fig. 6f,g). Together, our analyses across DNA methylation, chromatin accessibility and histone PTMs indicate that the basal-like subpopulation exhibts a noisy epigenetic landscape and increased transcriptional heterogeneity.

Our CyTOF analysis highlighted a global increase in several histone PTMs in the basal-like subpopulation, including H3K4 monomethylation and trimethylation (Fig. 2e). To explore the genomic distribution of these marks, we conducted single-nucleus CUT&Tag (snCUT&Tag) on three luminal tumours from our cohort60. Similar to the CyTOF data (Fig. 1b), stroma cells clustered together across patients, showing H3K4me1 and H3K4me3 deposition on fibroblast and endothelial markers. By contrast, tumours clustered separately, which indicated inter-patient variability (Extended Data Fig. 8a–d).

In each tumour, malignant cells clustered into distinct H3K4me1-defined or H3K4me3-defined states (Fig. 3e and Extended Data Fig. 8e,f). Differential analysis of H3K4me1 distribution between clusters highlighted a recurrent group of cells across tumours, annotated as ‘cluster 2’, with significant H3K4me1 enrichment at genes associated with basal-like identity and EMT (Fig. 3f,g and Extended Data Fig. 8g,i). In tumour 15, cluster 1 was also enriched for basal-like genes (adjusted P < 0.05), but not EMT. H3K4me3 similarly identified basal-like subpopulations in all tumours (Fig. 3h and Extended Data Fig. 8h,i). Accordingly, peaks associated with these clusters showed enrichment for transcription factor motifs linked to EMT and basal-like identity (Supplementary Fig. 7a). Next, we trained a classifier to identify H3K4me1-marked and H3K4me3-marked genes that contribute to variation between the clusters. For both histone methylations, these genes were enriched in terms related to breast cancer cellular identity, including oestrogen signalling, basal-like and mesenchymal identity (Supplementary Fig. 7b–e). Overall, our analysis provides support for chromatin-defined cell states in luminal tumour cells, including a basal-like state distinguished by H3K4me1 and H3K4me3 distributions.

The above snCUT&Tag results aligned with the heterogeneity observed by CyTOF, which led us to compare the single-cell datasets and integrating both genomic and protein information. CyTOF-defined basal-like cells showed global increases in both H3K4 methylation marks. We reasoned that sequencing reads per nucleus may reflect global levels of the target modification. Single-cell epigenomic analyses generally assume similar global modification levels, discarding read-count information, as in our analysis above61 (Fig. 3e–h). Departing from this convention, we examined whether read counts capture additional aspects of epigenetic heterogeneity. Across all three tumours and both modifications, read counts negatively correlated with luminal identity signatures and positively with basal-like and mesenchymal signatures (Fig. 3i and Extended Data Fig. 9a,b). Consistently, cells with high read counts, potentially indicative of elevated global levels of H3K4me1 or H3K4me3, showed less enrichment of these active marks at luminal identity genes. Although requiring further validation, this direct comparison suggests that read counts may serve as proxy for global levels of histone modifications to capture additional aspects of epigenetic variation.

To further integrate these datasets, we label-transferred the CyTOF classification (Figs. 1 and 2) onto the H3K4me1 snCUT&Tag dataset. CyTOF-predicted basal-like populations were enriched in the basal-like clusters identified by H3K4me1 genomic profiling (Fig. 3e and Extended Data Fig. 9b). For tumour 15, cluster 1 was also predicted to comprise basal-like cells, consistent with its higher H3K4me1 deposition on basal-like-associated genes (Fig. 3g and Extended Data Fig. 9c). CyTOF-predicted basal-like cells also showed higher H3K4me1 deposition at EMT and basal-like gene signatures, which further confirmed their distinct epigenetic and functional features (Extended Data Fig. 9d). To validate these results, we sorted luminal PDX models and MCF7 cells by K5 expression, followed by H3K4me1 CUT&Tag. K5low-specific peaks were enriched near oestrogen signalling genes, whereas K5hi-specific peaks were associated with basal-like and mesenchymal programs, which confirmed the distinct H3K4me1 landscapes between subpopulations (Extended Data Fig. 9e). Together, the protein abundance and genomic distribution data implicate H3K4me1 and H3K4me3 as epigenetic determinants of the basal-like subpopulation in luminal tumours.

The repressive mark H3K9me2 was also identified as a strong contributor to the epigenetic basal-like signature (Fig. 2d,e). Thus, we conducted H3K9me2 snCUT&Tag on tumour 8, which was also profiled for H3K4me1. Given that H3K9me2 occupies large genomic regions, its distribution is not readily interpretable in relation to gene activity, especially in low-coverage single-cell datasets. We therefore leveraged the H3K4me1 data and trained a classifier, assuming opposing genomic distributions of enhancer-associated H3K4me1 and repressive H3K9me2 chromatin62,63, to identify malignant versus stromal cells (Extended Data Fig. 9f). We next clustered tumour cells by H3K9me2 genomic distribution and applied the same H3K4me1-based inference framework. This approach predicted strong enrichment of basal-like cells in cluster 4, consistent with elevated H3K9me2 deposition on oestrogen-related genes (Extended Data Fig. 9g–i). This cluster also showed the highest H3K9me2 read counts per nucleus, which provided support for its correspondence to the H3K9me2hi basal-like cells identified by CyTOF (Extended Data Fig. 9j). Overall, these analyses highlight an epigenetically distinct basal-like population with globally increased and redistributed active and repressive histone modifications over genes associated with luminal-basal identity and EMT.

Our multimodal analysis linked the chromatin landscape to intratumoural cell-state diversity. We next aimed to translate our tissue-level findings to a liquid biopsy test based on our single-molecule EPINUC technology, which profiles the epigenetics of plasma-isolated nucleosomes28,29. We tailored EPINUC for breast cancer by developing single-molecule systems to quantify the breast-tissue-related proteins K5, L1CAM and MUC1, and added the histone PTMs H4K16ac and H4K20me3 (refs. 64,65,66,67) (Fig. 4a, Supplementary Table 5 and Supplementary Fig. 8a–c). Nucleosomes from plasma were captured and their combinatorial modifications imaged by TIRF microscopy, whereas protein biomarkers were quantified in parallel single-molecule antibody-capture assays (Fig. 4a). The expanded 29-parameter panel was applied to a cohort of plasma from 77 women with luminal breast cancer and 30 healthy women, and the results revealed significant differences (Supplementary Table 6). For example, cancer samples contained more H3K9ac and H4K16ac nucleosomes (Fig. 4b). As PTMs were normalized to nucleosome abundance, these differences reflect the epigenetic state rather than tumour burden. We also used EPINUC to measure PTM ratios and co-occurrence, which revealed increased bivalent (H3K4me3 and H3K27me3) nucleosomes, as previously observed in colorectal cancer and pancreatic cancer28. Indeed, bivalency is altered across cancers68, and can prime drug-tolerant persister programs in breast cancer19.

L1CAM and MST1 were also elevated in plasma from patients with breast cancer, a result in agreement with the association of high MST1 with poor prognosis in ER+ tumours69 (Fig. 4b and Supplementary Fig. 8d). Multiple parameters differed between healthy individuals and patients diagnosed with early-stage (T1) low-burden tumours, which demonstrated the early detection sensitivity of this method (Fig. 4b). Predictive power scores (PPS) revealed the contribution of the newly measured H4 PTMs, selected on the basis of the CyTOF analysis, which illustrates the value of matched tissue–plasma profiling (Fig. 4c). Principal component analysis (PCA) of predictive features separated healthy individuals from patients with breast cancer, which highlights the ability of EPINUC to capture differences between these groups (Fig. 4d).

We next applied machine-learning-based classifiers to diagnose luminal breast cancer from EPINUC data. SHAP analysis of XGBoost models trained on all patients, or only stage T1 cases, identified multiple histone PTMs and protein biomarkers as informative (Fig. 4e). Notably, both models emphasized combinatorial features, particularly H4K16ac and H4K20me3 co-occurrence, thereby highlighting the ability of EPINUC to quantify such combinations. In particular, H4K16ac activates transcription of transposable elements70, which reside in H4K20me3 heterochromatin71, and because transposable elements are often upregulated in cancer, elevated H4K16ac and H4K20me3 might be a cancer-associated phenomenon. Finally, we applied several classifiers to assess the diagnostic contribution of the expanded EPINUC panel in discriminating healthy individuals from patients with cancer. Use the original 20 EPINUC parameters28 produced an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.85 (Supplementary Fig. 9a), whereas the expanded 29-parameter panel achieved 0.95, including among patients with early-stage T1 cancer (Fig. 4f,g). Unlike mammography, the sensitivity of which declines with dense breast tissue72,73, the features and performance of EPINUC were unaffected by different BI-RADS breast density scores, including patients with heterogeneous and extremely dense breast scores (Supplementary Fig. 9b,c). To assess the robustness of the EPINUC-based classifier, we applied the model trained on the original cohort (MAYO-1; Fig. 4f) to an independent, separately processed set of plasma samples collected 6–12 months later (MAYO-2). Following batch correction (Methods), the pre-trained model accurately distinguished healthy from luminal breast cancer, achieving an AUC of 0.98 and high classification accuracy (Extended Data Fig. 10a,b).

To generalize our findings, we analysed pretreatment plasma from patients with luminal breast cancer at two independent medical centres (Supplementary Table 6). EPINUC distinguished patients from healthy controls with high accuracy in both cohorts and showed comparable sensitivity and specificity in TNBC (Extended Data Fig. 10c–e). Pooling all luminal samples across centres (n = 188), a model trained on 75% of the data achieved an AUC of 0.96 and robustly classified the remaining 25% despite mixed sources and batches, a scenario that reflects real-world clinical settings (Fig. 4h, Extended Data Fig. 10f and Supplementary Fig. 10). Performance was similar for luminal A and luminal B tumours (Extended Data Fig. 10g). Although retrospective, these results support the use of high-resolution, multiparametric plasma epigenetic analyses for cancer diagnosis.

MAYO-1 comprised preoperative samples with at least 5 years of clinical follow-up, which enabled stratification by 5-year recurrence (Fig. 5a). Already at diagnosis, several EPINUC features differed between patients who were disease-free and patients who had relapsed disease. H3K4 monomethylation and trimethylation, associated with the aggressive basal-like subpopulation, were elevated in plasma of patients developing recurrent disease (Fig. 5b). H3K27me3 and H3K9ac were also elevated, perhaps reflecting other aggressive tumour or microenvironmental states, such as cycling cells that were particularly high for histone acetylations (Extended Data Fig. 1b). Nucleosomes modified with both H3K9ac and H3K4me1 were higher in the recurrence group, a result that further demonstrates the power of EPINUC in capturing these combinations (Fig. 5b). ER or PR status did not associate with relapse (Fisher’s exact test, P > 0.05), and the epigenetic signature persisted in tumours with the following characteristics: comparable ER and PR levels; only luminal A tumours; low-burden T1–T2 or grade 1–2 disease; and tumours without lymphovascular invasion (LVI). No EPINUC feature was significantly associated with histological grade, which indicates that there is prognostic information beyond known clinical parameters (Extended Data Fig. 11a–f).
